cards.title: Micro-yes signup step: ask for consent before email capture
cards.summary: Inserting a 'Do you want 10% off?' micro-commitment step before the email field can lift signup conversion, but must be split-tested per brand.
cards.use_when: Designing or A/B testing the newsletter/SMS signup form (popup or full page) for an ecommerce store.
steps: Add a step before the email opt-in that asks only a yes/no question, e.g. 'Do you want 10% off your first order?' with a single CTA button ('Yes please') and no input field.
Remove the email input field from this step; clicking the button submits the micro-form and advances to the real email opt-in, which triggers the welcome flow.
Keep microcopy under the button (e.g. 'No thanks, I'll pay full price', 'No spam guaranteed') to give an exit route.
Split-test the form with and without the micro-yes step and compare the signup conversion rate for your own brand.
Because the source reports that the micro-yes gives a spike in signups for most brands but some brands perform better without it, always validate rather than assume.
caveats: Benefit is brand-dependent; source explicitly says to split-test it.
The micro-yes is a lead-conversion (signup) tactic, not a purchase-conversion result.

cards.title: Signup form tests: delay, format, and audience size
cards.summary: Test popup delay, popup vs full page, and other form variables on total signups, not just signup rate.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the newsletter signup popup for an ecommerce store, deciding timing and format.
steps: Run a time-delay A/B test, e.g. 4 seconds vs 12 seconds, and track total number of signups, not only the signup rate.
Expect a shorter delay to lower the signup rate but possibly raise total signups because the form is shown to a larger audience.
Test a popup form against a full-page form and compare signup rate and total signups.
Test headline copy: 'Save 10% now', 'Get 10% now', 'Take 10% off now', 'Unlock 10% off now', 'Your discount awaits', 'Do you want 10% off'.
Test CTA button text: 'Save 10% off now', 'Get 10% off now', 'Unlock my discount now', 'Reveal my discount now', 'I want my discount'.
Test microcopy variants such as 'No thanks, I'll pay full price', 'No sales spam guaranteed', 'Rated 4.9/5 by 5,000 customers'.
caveats: Signup rate and total signups can move in opposite directions; the source stresses watching total volume.
Exact lift numbers are not promised; treat headline/CTA effects as testable, not guaranteed.

cards.title: Visual signup form tests: color, images, and imagery content
cards.summary: Test plain vs designed, light vs dark, contrasting fields, and image presence/content on the signup form.
cards.use_when: Designing the visual layout of an ecommerce newsletter popup or signup page.
steps: Split-test a plain simple form against a fully designed form.
Split-test a white form against a black form, and test input-field colors (contrasting color vs plain white).
Test the CTA button color.
Split-test a centered form with no side image against a form with a side image.
When using images, test image content: the source cites a blanket brand where a blanket with a dog on it outperformed a plain blanket image.
caveats: The blanket-with-dog result is a single brand example, not a universal benchmark.
Image relevance to the product/category may matter more than image presence alone.

cards.title: SMS opt-in angles after email signup
cards.summary: Test offer-equivalence vs upgraded offer vs VIP-club angle for the SMS opt-in step.
cards.use_when: Adding or optimizing an SMS list opt-in step within the email signup flow.
steps: Build the SMS signup as an extra step after the email opt-in.
Angle 1: use the same offer for SMS as email (e.g. 10% off both), and test it.
Angle 2: offer a better SMS-only offer, e.g. email signup says 10% off, next step says 'Do you want 15% off? Sign up for SMS', and test it.
Angle 3: use a VIP Club angle — email opt-in offers 10% off, SMS step offers 'Join our VIP Club for exclusive sales, pre-sales, early access', and test it.
Split-test the angles against each other and measure SMS opt-in rate.
caveats: The source presents these as testable angles, not guaranteed winners.
Higher SMS discounts can erode margin; choose based on your own unit economics.

cards.title: Flow structure and profile filters in Klaviyo
cards.summary: Understand flow triggers, profile filters (order/cart/checkout exclusions), and profile properties to prevent overlapping emails.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing Klaviyo flows for an ecommerce store so customers don't receive conflicting sequences.
steps: Pick a trigger based on customer journey stage: active on site, viewed product, added to cart, checkout started, placed order, or added to list/segment.
After confirming a trigger, note it cannot be changed without duplicating the flow.

Add profile filters under the trigger, e.g. 'has placed order 0 times since starting this flow', 'has checkout started 0 times since starting this flow', 'has added to cart 0 times since starting this flow'.
For welcome series, add 'placed order 0 times', 'checkout started 0 times', and 'added to cart 0 times since starting this flow' so buyers and cart/checkout abandoners exit the welcome sequence.
Consider excluding 'viewed product' and 'active on site' as well, but source prefers not to exclude those from welcome since browse/site abandonment flows are short and early in the journey.
Use profile property updates (e.g. set 'in_welcome_series = true' at flow start, false at end) to segment flow participants in or out of regular campaigns.
Use conditional splits with 'placed order since starting flow' to route buyers to a post-purchase email vs continuing the welcome series, or use a random 50/50 split to A/B test flow strategies.
caveats: Trigger choice is locked after confirmation; you must duplicate the flow to change it.
Excluding checkout-started and added-to-cart from a welcome series is the source's preferred approach but is presented as a judgment call.

cards.title: Use past profiles to backfill newly launched flows
cards.summary: Backfill a new flow so eligible customers enter at the correct stage instead of waiting for the delay to elapse.
cards.use_when: Launching a winback, re-engagement, or time-delayed flow and wanting it to act on past behavior immediately.
steps: Open the flow's Manage Flow settings and choose 'Add past profiles'.
Choose 'throughout the flow' so profiles are added based on where they would be if the flow had been live earlier, rather than only at the beginning.

Example: a winback flow triggered 90 days after last order — adding past profiles throughout the flow lets someone whose last order was 80 days ago receive the first email in 10 days instead of waiting 90 days.
Select 'eligible profiles' as the whole list or a specific segment.
Note that flows containing dynamic coupons cannot use past profiles; if you need past profiles and a discount, use a static code instead.
caveats: Past-profile backfill is unavailable for dynamic coupon flows — a real trade-off if you rely on dynamic codes.
Adding profiles to the beginning vs throughout the flow produces very different behavior; choose deliberately.

cards.title: Turn off smart sending for flows, keep it on for campaigns
cards.summary: Disable smart sending in flows so abandoned-cart/checkout emails aren't skipped; keep it enabled for campaigns.
cards.use_when: Configuring send settings inside any Klaviyo flow email for an ecommerce store.
steps: In each flow email's settings, uncheck 'Skip recently emailed profile' (smart sending) and save.
Rationale: if a customer already received a campaign or other email within the last 16 hours, smart sending would skip them from a cart abandonment flow — losing high-intent, high-revenue sends.
For campaigns, keep smart sending on in ~99.9% of cases unless there's a specific reason to disable it.
The default smart-sending window is 16 hours and can be edited in general email settings (e.g. 8 hours), but the flow-level decision stays the same: off for flows.
Enable UTM tracking in the same settings block (and optionally custom tracking) so revenue and behavior attribution works with Google Analytics.
caveats: Source treats 'off for flows, on for campaigns' as its own strong rule; validate against your own send-frequency and deliverability data.
Disabling smart sending can increase total email volume, which matters for spam-complaint rates.

cards.title: Welcome series structure: 7 emails with distinct angles
cards.summary: Build a welcome series that delivers the incentive fast, then rotates through brand story, bestsellers, reviews, USP comparison, and expiring-discount urgency.
cards.use_when: Building or rewriting the welcome flow for an ecommerce store after newsletter signup.
steps: Email 1: deliver the discount code immediately (the promised incentive).
Email 2 (~1 day later): brand story — founder message, origin, mission, what sets you apart — to build trust before pushing product.
Email 3 (~1 day later): bestsellers; dive into unique features/benefits and the end result for the customer; cap at ~3–5 bestsellers depending on brand.
Email 4 (~2 days later): reviews/UGC/press mentions — prioritize reviews about the specific pain points your subscriber has, not generic 'highly recommended' quotes.
Email 5 (~2 days later): 'us vs them' USP comparison, since subscribers are comparing you to competitors.
Email 6 (~2 days later): either a 48-hour discount reminder or a new/higher discount with a 48-hour deadline (source's split of two routes).
Email 7 (~1 day later): 24-hour discount expiry as a plain-text email from the founder — plain text tends to improve deliverability and adds a personal touch.
Remind subscribers of the discount code in every email, but give each email its own distinct angle.
Add profile filters (placed order, checkout started, added to cart = 0 since starting flow) so buyers and cart/checkout abandoners exit the welcome series.
caveats: The 3-day and 4-day defaults from Klaviyo are presented as slower than the source's preference; both are options, not proven superior.
Fake urgency is explicitly cautioned against — make sure stated deadlines are real.
Timing and email count are the source's opinion, not tested benchmarks.

cards.title: Site abandonment flow: trigger, delay, and one guiding email
cards.summary: Build a site-abandonment flow for visitors who never viewed a product, using the active-on-site trigger and a 1–4 hour delay.
cards.use_when: Recovering early-stage site visitors (homepage/blog visitors who did not view a product) for an ecommerce store.
steps: Create a flow with the 'active on site' API trigger.
Add profile filters: 'has placed order 0 times', 'checkout started 0 times', 'added to cart 0 times', and 'viewed product 0 times since starting this flow' so anyone advancing in the journey exits.
Add a time delay before email 1 of 1–4 hours; source suggests earlier journey stages can wait longer.
Send one email that acts as a shop assistant: 'Is this what you're looking for?' with links to relevant collections or specific products depending on your catalog size.
A/B test 1 hour vs 4 hours, and test 'guide to collections' vs 'guide to bestsellers' to see which drives product views.
Turn off smart sending and enable UTM tracking in the email settings.
caveats: The flow normally has a single email because these visitors are early in the journey and not yet high-intent.
No default Klaviyo template exists for site abandonment; you must build it yourself.

cards.title: Browse abandonment flow: trigger, filters, and review-led emails
cards.summary: Set up a browse-abandonment flow triggered by viewed product, with product-specific reviews and a discount only after several emails.
cards.use_when: Re-engaging shoppers who viewed a product but never added to cart on an ecommerce store.
steps: Use the 'viewed product' trigger.
Add profile filters: 'checkout started 0 times', 'placed order 0 times', 'added to cart 0 times since starting this flow', and 'has not been in flow for the last 30 days'.
Set the first-email delay — Klaviyo defaults to 2 hours; test 1 hour vs 3 hours and narrow down.
Email 1: simple 'Did you see something you like?' reminder of the viewed product.
Email 2 (~1 day later): reviews, UGC, press mentions to build confidence in the specific product.
Use trigger filters to build product- or collection-specific browse flows, and make USP/review content specific to the viewed product — the source says specificity converts better.
Delay any discount until around email 4–5; source argues giving discounts immediately trains shoppers to wait for codes.
Aim for a 4–6 email sequence; turn off smart sending and enable UTM tracking.
caveats: 'Wait to discount' is the source's opinion, not a tested benchmark across all stores.
The 30-day flow suppression window is a default recommendation; your repurchase cycle and catalog should guide the choice.

cards.title: Abandoned cart flow: trigger distinction and 6–8 email structure
cards.summary: Build a true added-to-cart abandonment flow (not the mislabeled checkout default) with a 30-minute-to-2-hour delay and staged email angles.
cards.use_when: Setting up or fixing the abandoned cart sequence for an ecommerce store in Klaviyo.
steps: Select a Klaviyo template whose trigger is 'added to cart' — the popular 'abandoned cart' template actually uses 'checkout started', so verify the trigger before building.

Add profile filters: 'checkout started 0 times', 'placed order 0 times', and 'has not been in flow for the last X days' (Klaviyo defaults to 7 days; source prefers ~14 days, adjusting for repurchase frequency).
Set the first-email delay to 30 minutes–2 hours (Klaviyo default 4 hours is described as long), and A/B test 30 minutes vs 2 hours.
Email 1: short reminder that the item is still in cart.
Email 2 (~1 day later): reviews/UGC/press — the more specific to the exact product, the better.
Email 3: objection handling — address reasons someone might hesitate to finish the purchase.
Email 4: specific USPs of the product/brand.
Email 5 (~1 day later): first discount (e.g. X% off) with 48-hour urgency, because a discount without urgency gives no reason to buy now.
Email 6 (~1 day later): 24-hour deadline reminder.
Emails 7–8 options: raise the discount, or send a plain-text founder email offering an extended 24-hour sale.
Monitor spam-complaint, unsubscribe, and open rates as you lengthen the sequence; source warns long sequences (14–20+ emails) become annoying.
caveats: Sources disagree on sequence length and suppression windows; treat 6–8 emails and 14 days as source preferences, not industry standards.
Discounts should reflect margin realities; the source explicitly ties higher discounts to margins.
Adding a post-purchase branch inside the cart flow is described as a common but not recommended pattern — the source prefers separate flows.

cards.title: Checkout abandonment flow: same structure, different objections
cards.summary: Clone the abandoned cart flow and retarget checkout starters with content tailored to late-stage objections like shipping costs.
cards.use_when: Recovering shoppers who started checkout but did not complete the purchase on an ecommerce store.
steps: Clone the abandoned cart flow and change its trigger to 'checkout started'.
Remove the 'checkout started 0 times' profile filter (no longer relevant); keep 'placed order 0 times since starting this flow' and the flow-suppression window.
Reuse the cart sequence structure but tailor copy to checkout-stage objections — the source cites surprise shipping costs as a common blocker.
Consider offering free shipping instead of a percentage discount when shipping is the likely objection; source argues free shipping can cost less (for a $200 AOV) while converting the customer.
Adjust reviews, USP content, and discount amounts to the later stage; these customers are one step closer to purchase.
Keep discount timing late in the sequence (around email 5) and use urgency with any discount.
caveats: The free-shipping-vs-discount trade-off depends on your margins and AOV; source gives a $200 AOV example, not a universal rule.
Separate cart and checkout flows are both needed; do not rely on a single 'abandoned cart' template for both.

cards.title: Time-delay heuristics by journey stage
cards.summary: First-email delays should shorten as the customer moves from browsing to checkout, and each delay should be split-tested.
cards.use_when: Setting or tuning the first-email delay inside ecommerce abandonment flows.
steps: Site abandonment (no product viewed): 1–4 hours.
Browse abandonment (product viewed): ~1–3 hours; Klaviyo default ~2 hours.
Cart abandonment (added to cart): 30 minutes–2 hours; Klaviyo default 4 hours described as too long.
Checkout abandonment: shortest delay, since intent is highest (structure follows cart flow with faster timing).
Run A/B tests at each stage (e.g. 1 hour vs 4 hours for site abandonment) and narrow toward the best-performing delay.

Inside time delays, you can also delay until a specific time of day or weekday, and choose store timezone, recipient local timezone, or specific days — use these to align sends with typical browsing/buying times.
caveats: These are source heuristics, not tested universal timings — the source repeatedly says to split-test.
Correct timing depends on niche, audience, and purchase frequency.

cards.title: Subject line, preview text, and sender name optimization
cards.summary: Treat preview text as a second subject line, test sender names, and keep sender email consistent across all sends.
cards.use_when: Configuring email metadata for ecommerce flows and campaigns in Klaviyo.
steps: In each email's edit settings, fill in subject line, preview text, sender name, and sender email address.
Write a distinct, compelling preview text — the source calls it your second subject line; do not skip it.
Note that plain-text emails have no preview text field, so only the subject line applies.
Test sender name variants, e.g. a founder's name vs the company name, especially in welcome series.
Use the same sender email address across all flows and campaigns to protect deliverability and consistency.
Preview the email in desktop and mobile views before publishing.
caveats: Plain-text emails can't use preview text, so you must rely on subject line alone — plan accordingly.
No specific subject-line lift figures are given; treat this as a testable area.

cards.title: Bulk flow action status and flow analytics
cards.summary: Use flow-level settings to publish/draft all emails at once and analyze flow performance over custom time frames.
cards.use_when: Managing, launching, or reviewing ecommerce email flows in Klaviyo.
steps: In the flow's Manage Flow settings, update action statuses to set all emails to live, manual, or draft at once rather than editing each email individually.
Add flow name and tags to keep flows organized.
Use the Show Analytics view and select a time frame (including custom) to review flow performance.
Use flow history to see changes over time.
Note that trigger selection is permanent at the flow level; to change a trigger, duplicate the flow.
caveats: Bulk status changes apply to all emails in the flow — verify no email is intentionally paused before switching to live.
Klaviyo's interface changes frequently (the source notes the company was running UX tests in 2024), so verify current menu locations.

cards.title: Decide whether to use Klaviyo's default flow templates
cards.summary: Klaviyo's prebuilt templates are a starting point for beginners, but custom-built flows typically convert better.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to start an ecommerce flow from a Klaviyo template or build from scratch.
steps: When creating a flow, browse Klaviyo's prebuilt flows by goal (e.g. prevent lost sales, nurture subscribers) if you lack email marketing experience.
Recognize that default templates are not optimized for your specific brand and audience.
If you have the capability, build custom flows from scratch; the source recommends this approach for better conversion.
If you do use a template, review and adjust triggers, delays, and content before launching — never ship a template unedited.
Note the source's view: something is better than nothing, but custom flow work is worth the effort.
caveats: 'Custom flows convert better than templates' is the source's opinion, not a measured benchmark.
Template availability and naming in Klaviyo change; verify current options in the interface.

cards.title: Exclude engaged customers from overlapping flows
cards.summary: Use profile filters so customers advance to the next journey stage without receiving overlapping flows.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing ecommerce email flow logic to prevent a customer receiving conflicting or repetitive sequences.
steps: For each pre-purchase flow, add exclusion filters for later journey events: e.g. welcome series excludes placed order, checkout started, and added to cart.
Site abandonment excludes placed order, checkout started, added to cart, and viewed product since starting the flow.
Browse abandonment excludes checkout started, placed order, and added to cart since starting the flow.
Cart abandonment excludes checkout started and placed order since starting the flow.
Checkout abandonment excludes only placed order since starting the flow.
Set a 'has not been in flow for the last X days' filter (30 days for browse, 7–14 days for cart/checkout) to prevent re-triggering the same flow too often.
Rationale: overlapping flows send too many emails, which can trigger spam complaints and erode trust.
caveats: Whether to exclude active-on-site and viewed-product from the welcome series is a judgment call; source prefers not to exclude those because their flows are short.
Flow-suppression windows should match your repurchase cycle — a 7-day window is fine for weekly replenishment but too short for long repurchase cycles.

cards.title: Use trigger filters for product- and collection-specific flows
cards.summary: Trigger filters let you limit browse/cart abandonment flows to specific products or collections for more relevant messaging.
cards.use_when: Building product-specific or collection-specific abandonment sequences in Klaviyo for an ecommerce catalog.
steps: Open the flow's trigger settings and add a trigger filter under Add trigger filter.
Select dimensions to include or exclude specific products or collections — e.g. only send a browse-abandonment flow for a high-margin collection.
Use trigger filters when you want different sequences for different product categories, each with its own reviews, USPs, and objections.
For site abandonment flows, trigger filters are generally not used because no product has been viewed yet.
Combine trigger filters with specific review/UGC content about the exact product or collection to increase relevance.
caveats: The more product-specific flows you build, the more maintenance overhead; prioritize products/collections with enough traffic to justify it.
Klaviyo's trigger-filter UI may move between versions; verify current setup in the interface.

cards.title: Use plain-text founder emails and real urgency for final conversion
cards.summary: End long flows with a plain-text founder email that carries real, verifiable urgency rather than a designed template.
cards.use_when: Writing the final emails of ecommerce welcome, cart, checkout, or browse sequences to convert holdouts.
steps: Send the final email as plain text rather than a designed template — the source says plain text generally delivers better and feels more personal.
Send it from the founder's name (a real or fictional person at the company), using the founder's voice.
Use explicit urgency such as 'your discount expires in 24 hours', and make it true — the source stresses not using fake urgency.
For discount expiry, use a dynamic coupon code so the deadline is genuine; avoid static codes like 'WELCOME10' as the urgency mechanism.
Options for the final push: extended sale for 24 hours only, a higher discount, or a founder plain-text last-chance email.
In welcome series, place this plain-text founder email around email 7; in cart/checkout flows, use it around emails 6–8.
caveats: Fake urgency damages trust; use dynamic codes or genuinely expiring offers.
Plain-text emails cannot include preview text, so the subject line carries the full burden.
